messages.subject: Re: Code for outlie()
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ollie,

You would want something vaguely like this:

for(i in 1:length(ANIMAL))
{
  OUT <- outlie(ANIMAL[[i]],plot=FALSE)
  BAD <- OUT$speed > THRESHOLD
  while(BAD)
  {
    ANIMAL[[i]] <- ANIMAL[[i]][!BAD,]
    OUT <- outlie(ANIMAL[[i]],plot=FALSE)
    BAD <- OUT$speed > THRESHOLD
  }
}

Best,
Chris

If you have resting data in different locations, then the time in between those segments needs to be expanded so that the rest speed could have explained those transitions.
With future behavioral switching models, this will not be necessary. But when fitting one stationary model at a time, it needs to be able to explain all of the segmented data.

Best,
Chris

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Charlotte,

The projection argument of as.telemetry() is for the output coordinates: help('as.telemetry') <https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/as.telemetry.html>

For data frames, the input data are assumed to be in Movebank format, which would either have the input coordinates in long-lat (potentially needing the datum argument) or in UTM with a UTM zone column. Alternatively, if the input data are in an sp-based move object, then they can be in any projection.

After you have your data imported into a telemetry object, you can see the projection information with projection() <https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/projection.html> and you can also export <https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/export.html> the data into formats for use in QGIS.

Not seeing any other messages or warnings, I'm assuming your data contained long-lat coordinates, which were imported and projected to epsg:32630.

Best,
Chris

Hi Mike,
Riemann integration should be faster on a stationary model, and shouldn't run out of RAM if it works, but it needs the rasters to be in a consistent lattice and the resolution cannot be too coarse.
There is a max.mem argument that you can set for Monte-Carlo integration, so that the calculation can finish without an OOM error. The final numerical precision estimate is stored in the fit object.
I don't think that cropping should speed anything up, unless the full raster is too big to keep in RAM without cropping, in which case that might help some.
Formula objects just look like ~ trees + land_use and rsf.select() will build up and then pair down the different predictors to try and find the best combination.
Try adding  + offset(land) to your formula. This is not as strenuously tested, so tell me if it doesn't work.
I will be switching from raster to terra in the next year, but I don't think that will be making much difference, because I think the two packages are basically calling the same functions at this point.
Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I have a question about creating seasonal RSFs and I just wanted to check that I understand the correct approach.

We are wanting to assess the influence of study area/population level factors (including the presence or not of wolves, bears, and/or puma hunting by humans) on the selection of critical habitat characteristics (specifically feeding/kill sites and bed sites) of pumas. We have GPS collar data for multiple pumas across multiple study areas in both North and South America and multiple kill and bed sites for each puma. Study areas are exposed to differing combinations of external factors (i.e. wolves, bears, humans). So, we are more interested in what is happening at a population level per study area rather than at the individual puma level. I understand we can derive population level parameters from RSFs by placing individual estimates in a list and calculating mean().

Given the presence of bears and hunting are seasonal, it would seem prudent that we create seasonal RSFs. Below is a potential workflow:

Habitat selection per seasonal home range:
- Split all movement/location data for each puma according to season (e.g. winter vs summer)
- Calculate akdes per season
- Create separate RSFs for winter and summer for each individual, using seasonal akdes and location data (I think NDVI will be the only time dependent variable being used in the RSFS, so we should use mean summer NDVI for summer RSF, and use mean winter NDVI for winter RSF)
- Calculate population level/study area RSF parameter estimates using mean()

Habitat selection for bed and kill sites per season:
- Split kill and bed sites by season
- Create separate RSFs for winter and summer for each individual for kill sites and bed sites, using seasonal akdes and kill and bed site locations
- Calculate population level/study area RSF parameter estimates using mean()

Hence, I was thinking of creating the following 9 RSFs per individual before deriving population level parameter estimates:
1. all locations
2. all kill sites
3. all bed sites
4. winter only locations
5. winter only kill sites
6. winter only bed sites
7. summer locations
8. summer kill sites
9. summer bed sites

Questions:
1. Is the above workflow appropriate to account for potential seasonal differences in habitat selection by pumas?

2. If an individual puma is monitored across multiple years and therefore multiple seasons (e.g. 3 winters and 2 summers), do I need to calculate individual akdes per season per year (i.e. 1st akde for winter 1, 2nd akde for winter 2, 3rd akde for winter 3, etc) and then calculate the mean akde before RSF fitting, to account for the large gap in time between seasons and the influence on range-residency assumption? Or can I just create a single seasonal akde from the beginning, despite a large time gap between the same season across multiple years?

3. If I want to assess seasonal habitat selection, do I need to first create a seasonal akde (i.e. Winter kill site selection should only be assessed relative to winter akde, not the entire akde across all seasons)?

Regards,
Luke.

messages.subject: Re: AKDE of one behavior type
messages.body_plain:
Hi Maxime,

You can do a simple comparison of the mean dive speed compared to the distance between dive areas divided by the time gaps to fly between them.

In another species where birds forage on foot, then the mean foraging speed would be very low compared to the distance between foraging patches divided by the time gaps to fly between them, and you really have to make some adjustment (like expanding the time between) to fit one stationary model to that data. In this case, the gap times need to be expanded sufficiently so that the birds could have walked on foot from one patch to another (even though they don't do that).

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Dear Christen,

Thank you very much for getting back to me so quickly. I have tried to play around with 'dt,' but I have not got around to it as yet, that is, specifying the right time-lag bin width. Our sampling regime was irregular because we took GPS fixes every time the birds moved - that is, once we spotted the bird, we recorded the time, watched its activity at a safe distance and then took GPS coordinates once it moved to another foraging patch. I have, however, used the shiny APP to check the variogram for this individual, and this is what it looks like (attached photo).

The effective sample size for this individual is 15, and the absolute sample size is 47 ( it was spending a lot of time in each foraging patch). This individual was tracked for 18 hours ( that is within 6 days, for 3 hours each day). Given that the variogram somehow flattens with an increasing time lag, am I right to say that this bird has been tracked 'enough' to show range residency, and thus we can calculate home ranges?
I will highly appreciate your thoughts.

Thank you,
Gladys.
